description: We are Team Anatolith! 🚀 Our name bridges the cradle of earthly civilization (Anatolia) with the frontier of space exploration (Regolith). We are a passionate team combining software development, UI/UX, and game design skills. We believe that great design, solid code, and immersive storytelling are the ultimate tools for exploring the unknown.
summary: Station 13: Mission Control is a 2D aerospace engineering and mission operations simulation built in Godot 4 for 1-4 players. Inspired by real NASA missions, players act as mission control engineers tasked with designing, assembling, and launching spacecraft under strict budget, mass, power, and thermal constraints. Instead of static menus, players physically navigate a facility to align launch windows, wire power busbars, haul cargo, and manage deep-space communications. Mid-mission emergencies, like solar flares, are resolved deterministically based on the spacecraft’s actual build rather than luck, turning complex aerospace trade-offs into an engaging and educational cooperative experience.
details:
Station 13: Mission Control

What It Does & How It Works: A 2D aerospace engineering simulation built in Godot 4 for 1-4 players. Players act as mission control, designing and launching spacecraft for 4 NASA-inspired missions (LEO, Moon, Jupiter, Mars). Instead of static menus, players physically navigate a station: aligning orbits, wiring power busbars, buying payloads on a strict budget, and launching. Mid-mission crises (e.g., solar flares) are resolved deterministically based on the ship's actual build (power reserves, mass margins) rather than luck.

Tools Used: Godot Engine 4, GDScript (event-driven architecture), JSON (for modular data), Godot RPC (multiplayer), and Git.

Creativity: It turns dry spreadsheet-based engineering into a tactile experience. Players physically carry cargo crates and manually fix tripped wires, blending gamified mechanics with authentic aerospace systems.

Benefits & Impact: Makes aerospace engineering, resource trade-offs, and mission operations exciting for students. It visually teaches why real space missions require careful planning, redundancy, and collaborative teamwork.

Factors Considered: Scientific realism (managing deep-space solar drops and temperatures), fairness (eliminating pure randomness from crises), game balance (rocket upgrades cost budget to force strategic trade-offs), and clear UX/UI.
